meta.titre: Rates of Reaction: collisions, factors and reading graphs

sections.contenu_markdown: In the hot kitchen of a restaurant in Bamenda, the cook splits firewood into thin sticks to make the fire catch quickly, and she grinds dry pepper to a powder so that it dissolves in the soup within seconds. Some changes happen in a flash, such as a match striking, while others take years, such as iron roofing sheets rusting. Chemists measure how fast a reaction goes and learn how to speed it up or slow it down. This is useful in factories, in food storage and in medicine, which is why questions on the factors affecting reaction rate, on graphs and on gas collection appear almost every year in the GCE Ordinary Level chemistry papers.

items: All matter is made of particles that are in constant motion, and they move faster when the temperature rises.
A chemical reaction changes reactants into new substances called products.
A balanced equation shows the mole ratio in which substances react.
Concentration tells how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution, for example in mol per $\mathrm{dm^3}$.

sections.titre: Rate of reaction, collision theory and the five factors
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Rate of reaction** is how fast reactants are used up or products are formed. It is found by measuring a change during a time interval:

$$\text{average rate} = \frac{\text{change in amount of product (or reactant)}}{\text{time taken}}$$

Typical units are $\mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$ (gas volume), $\mathrm{g\ s^{-1}}$ (mass) or $\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}$.

**Collision theory.** A reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy (the *activation energy*). A faster reaction means more successful collisions per second.

| Factor | Change | Effect on rate | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concentration (solutions) or pressure (gases) | increased | faster | more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions |
| Temperature | increased | faster | particles move faster, collide more often and with more energy, so more collisions are successful |
| Surface area of a solid | larger (powder instead of lumps) | faster | more particles exposed to the other reactant |
| Catalyst | added | faster | gives an easier pathway with lower activation energy |
| Light (some reactions) | stronger | faster | supplies energy, e.g. silver chloride turning grey |

**Measuring the rate.** (1) Collect gas in a gas syringe (or an upturned measuring cylinder over water) and read the volume at regular times. (2) Place the flask on a balance and record the loss of mass as gas escapes. (3) Time how long a mark seen through the mixture takes to disappear when a precipitate forms.

**Reading a graph** of product against time: the steeper the line, the faster the reaction. The curve flattens when one reactant is used up, and the final level depends only on the amount of the limiting reactant.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question says a substance speeds up a reaction but is not used up.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A catalyst increases the rate but is chemically unchanged at the end and its mass stays the same. Only a small amount is needed and it does not change the amount of product. Examples: manganese(IV) oxide in $2\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$; iron in the Haber process; vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When two experiments are drawn on the same axes.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A steeper curve means a faster reaction (higher concentration, higher temperature, smaller particles or a catalyst). If the same amount of the limiting reactant is used, both curves finish at the **same final volume**, but the faster one reaches it earlier. If less of the limiting reactant is used, the curve finishes at a lower level.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student adds 0.30 g of marble chips ($\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$) to an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid. The gas is collected in a gas syringe at room temperature and its volume is read every 10 seconds.

| Time (s) | Total volume of gas ($\mathrm{cm^3}$) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 30 |
| 20 | 48 |
| 30 | 60 |
| 40 | 68 |
| 50 | 72 |
| 60 | 72 |

(a) Write a balanced equation. (b) Calculate the average rate over the first 10 s and between 30 s and 40 s. (c) At what time did the reaction stop? (d) Explain why the rate decreases as time passes. (e) Show that the final volume agrees with the mass of marble used.

etapes.justification: The gas given off is carbon dioxide from the carbonate.

etapes.action: Find the average rate over the first 10 s.
etapes.justification: Rate = volume change divided by time.

etapes.action: Find the average rate between 30 s and 40 s.
etapes.justification: Use the volumes at 30 s and 40 s.
When the reaction is over, the volume no longer changes.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The volume stays at $72\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ from 50 s onwards, so the reaction stopped at **50 s**.

etapes.justification: The rate depends on the number of collisions, and this falls as the reactant particles are used up.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The marble chips get smaller and the acid becomes less concentrated, so there are fewer collisions per second and the curve becomes less steep.

etapes.justification: Moles of marble, then moles of gas, then volume at 24 $\mathrm{dm^3}$ per mole.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $n(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = \dfrac{0.30}{100} = 0.003\ \mathrm{mol}$, so $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 0.003\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $V = 0.003 \times 24\,000 = 72\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, which matches the graph.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The average rate falls from $3.0$ to $0.8\ \mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$ because the reactants are used up, the reaction stops at 50 s, and the final volume of $72\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ is fixed by the $0.30\ \mathrm{g}$ of marble, the limiting reactant.

items.erreur_markdown: "The rate of a reaction is the total volume of gas produced."
items.pourquoi_faux: The total volume tells how much product is made, not how fast it is made. Rate involves time.
items.correction_markdown: Rate = change in volume divided by the time taken, for example in $\mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$.

items.erreur_markdown: "A catalyst is used up during the reaction, so it must be replaced."
items.pourquoi_faux: A catalyst takes part in the reaction but is regenerated, so it is chemically unchanged and its mass is the same at the end.
items.correction_markdown: A catalyst speeds up the reaction by lowering the activation energy and can be recovered unchanged.

items.erreur_markdown: "Lumps of marble react faster than powder because lumps have more mass."
items.pourquoi_faux: What matters is the surface area exposed to the acid, not the mass of the piece. Powder exposes far more surface.
items.correction_markdown: The same mass of powder reacts faster than lumps because more particles are in contact with the acid.

items.erreur_markdown: "Doubling the concentration of the acid gives double the final volume of gas."
items.pourquoi_faux: The final volume is fixed by the amount of the limiting reactant. A higher concentration only makes the reaction faster.
items.correction_markdown: If the acid is in excess, the final volume is the same; the curve is simply steeper and finishes earlier.

items.erreur_markdown: "At a higher temperature the reaction is faster only because the particles move faster."
items.pourquoi_faux: This is incomplete. Faster particles collide more often, but the main reason is that a larger fraction of the collisions has the activation energy.
items.correction_markdown: State both points: more frequent collisions and more collisions with enough energy to react.

items.enonce_markdown:
Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Four experiments are carried out with the same mass of magnesium.

| Experiment | Magnesium | Acid concentration ($\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}$) | Temperature ($^\circ$C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | ribbon | 1.0 | 25 |
| B | ribbon | 2.0 | 25 |
| C | powder | 1.0 | 25 |
| D | ribbon | 1.0 | 45 |

(a) Name the factor changed in B, C and D compared with A. (b) Which experiment is the slowest? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) B: **concentration** of the acid. C: **surface area** of the magnesium (powder instead of ribbon). D: **temperature**.

(b) Experiment **A** is the slowest. Each of B, C and D has one change that increases the number of successful collisions (more particles per volume, more exposed surface, faster particles), while A has the lowest concentration, the smallest surface area and the lowest temperature.

items.enonce_markdown:
Hydrogen peroxide solution is decomposed by manganese(IV) oxide: $2\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} + \mathrm{O_{2}}$. The oxygen is collected and measured.

| Time (s) | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total volume of oxygen ($\mathrm{cm^3}$) | 0 | 36 | 60 | 72 | 72 |

(a) Calculate the average rate in the first 20 s and between 40 s and 60 s. (b) Why is the second rate smaller? (c) What mass of hydrogen peroxide was present at the start? (d) State what happens to the mass of manganese(IV) oxide.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) First 20 s: $\dfrac{36}{20} = 1.8\ \mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$. Between 40 s and 60 s: $\dfrac{72 - 60}{20} = 0.6\ \mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$.

(b) The hydrogen peroxide is being used up, so its concentration falls and there are fewer collisions per second.

(c) Final volume $72\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ so $n(\mathrm{O_2}) = \dfrac{72}{24\,000} = 0.003\ \mathrm{mol}$. From the equation 2 mol of $\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}$ gives 1 mol of $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, so $n(\mathrm{H_2O_2}) = 2 \times 0.003 = 0.006\ \mathrm{mol}$. Relative molecular mass: $2 + 32 = 34$. Mass $= 0.006 \times 34 = $ **0.204 g**.

(d) The mass of the catalyst is **unchanged**; it is not used up.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student reacts 0.65 g of zinc granules with 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of dilute sulphuric acid of concentration 1.0 $\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}$ at 25 $^\circ$C: $\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$. The reaction is complete after 120 s.

(a) Show that the acid is in excess and calculate the total volume of hydrogen produced. (b) Calculate the average rate over the whole reaction. (c) The experiment is repeated with the same mass of zinc powder. Give the final volume of hydrogen and say whether the reaction time is longer or shorter. (d) The first experiment is repeated with 0.325 g of zinc granules. State the final volume of hydrogen.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $n(\mathrm{Zn}) = \dfrac{0.65}{65} = 0.010\ \mathrm{mol}$. $n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = 1.0 \times 0.050 = 0.050\ \mathrm{mol}$. The ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.010 mol of acid is needed and 0.050 mol is available: the acid is in excess. $n(\mathrm{H_2}) = 0.010\ \mathrm{mol}$, so $V = 0.010 \times 24\,000 = $ **240 $\mathrm{cm^3}$**.

(b) Average rate $= \dfrac{240}{120} = $ **2.0 $\mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$**.

(c) The final volume is still **240 $\mathrm{cm^3}$** because the amount of zinc has not changed. The powder has a larger surface area, so the reaction is **shorter** (faster).

(d) $n(\mathrm{Zn}) = \dfrac{0.325}{65} = 0.005\ \mathrm{mol}$, so $V = 0.005 \times 24\,000 = $ **120 $\mathrm{cm^3}$** (half as much, because zinc is now the limiting reactant at half the amount).

items_markdown: Rate = change in amount of product (or reactant) divided by time taken; a steeper graph means a faster reaction.
Reactions need collisions with at least the activation energy; the five factors work by changing how often and how energetically particles collide.
Higher concentration (or pressure), higher temperature, larger surface area and a catalyst all increase the rate.
A catalyst is unchanged at the end and does not alter the amount of product.
The final volume of gas depends on the limiting reactant, never on the rate.
Rate can be followed by a gas syringe, by loss of mass on a balance, or by timing the disappearance of a mark.
